conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way.

I’ll be using a quick, well-trusted questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. Your answers are confidential, and nothing you share leaves this room unless you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else needs urgent help for safety.

We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no “right” or “wrong” replies. When we’re done, we’ll talk about what the score might mean and what supports could help you feel more like yourself again.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, most of the time it feels pretty difficult. I’ll smile if my partner or someone cracks a joke, but it fades fast. I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed—like, really laughed—since the baby came. Everything just feels heavy, so even funny things don’t land the way they used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh a little—maybe once or twice this week when my husband made one of his dumb jokes—but it’s not the same easy laugh I used to have. It feels kind of forced, like I have to remind myself to enjoy it, and then the smile just slips away.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I can still push myself to do a couple of things, and once I’m there I might feel a tiny spark, but the looking-forward part just isn’t there most days.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe my milk isn’t enough or I missed his cues. Even when the diaper leaks or he won’t nap, I hear this voice in my head saying I should’ve known better. I know, logically, babies just cry and mess up diapers, but I still feel like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much, yeah. My mind keeps running “what-if” loops—what if he spits up and chokes while I’m dozing off, what if the stroller tips, what if I’m missing some illness. There’s no real reason for most of it; he’s healthy and my midwife says he’s thriving. But the worry just sits there, and some nights I can’t shut it off long enough to fall asleep.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—like yesterday while I was folding laundry, my heart just started racing and I felt short-of-breath. Nothing had happened, but I got this sudden rush that something awful was about to happen to the baby or to me. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky. It’s only been a couple of times this week, but it’s scary when it hits.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish feeding, there’s laundry piled up, then he’s crying again, and I haven’t even brushed my teeth. I’ll look around the living room and just feel this wave of “I can’t keep up.” I still manage to get through it—he’s always fed and changed—but I’m running on fumes and feel like I’m drowning a little.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get him down, but then my mind starts replaying everything I think I did wrong or could go wrong, and I can’t settle. I lie there feeling sad and tense, and even when I do drift off I wake up again with those anxious thoughts. It’s like the unhappiness just buzzes in the background and won’t let my brain shut off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that’s most of the day, pretty much every day this week. It’s like this gray cloud hanging over me—I’ll be feeding the baby or just sitting on the couch and feel this heavy sadness. It’s not always sobbing, just this constant miserable, empty feeling that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple times—once this week when he wouldn’t settle for three hours straight and I felt completely useless, and another night after everyone was asleep and the house was finally quiet. It’s not all-day crying, but when everything piles up the tears just come and I can’t stop them for a while.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s crossed my mind once or twice, mostly at night when I’m exhausted and feel like I’m failing him. Nothing planned—just this fleeting “what if I weren’t here” thought, followed by guilt for even thinking it. I’d never act on it; I just want to feel like myself again.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy and gray-laughter comes rarely and feels forced, activities you once anticipated now feel like chores, and an endless loop of worries about your baby's safety keeps you awake even when he sleeps. You described sudden surges of panic, frequent tears, and a constant sense of failing him, all while running on fumes and still managing to care for him. These feelings are exhausting and frightening, and it's understandable to long for the lighter, more confident version of yourself you remember.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional, forced laughter this week—marked reduction from usual enjoyment.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, pervasive self-blame across multiple daily situations, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses pervasive, intrusive worries occurring frequently without cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes discrete episodes of sudden, intense fear and physical panic symptoms that occurred twice this week, matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent daily overwhelm, inability to keep up, and feeling of "drowning," indicating partial coping difficulty consistent with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sleep disturbance occurring "several nights this week" with persistent anxious rumination, sadness, tension, and repeated waking, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness that feels constant and heavy, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent fleeting self-harm thoughts, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. You endorse <sym>persistent sadness</sym>, <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>psychomotor agitation</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>recurrent thoughts of death</sym>, meeting core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Combined with frequent <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym> and <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>, immediate clinical evaluation is warranted. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health team to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Request a warm hand-off to a <med>therapist</med> skilled in <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression</med>
3. Ask your doctor about evidence-based treatments including <med>sertraline</med> or other <med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Create a written safety plan: list 24/7 crisis lines (e.g., 988), trusted contacts, and steps to take if suicidal thoughts intensify
5. Schedule daily 30-minute support blocks-partner, family, or friend to handle baby care so you can nap, shower, or rest without interruption
6. Begin gentle re-engagement: one 10-minute walk or pleasurable activity per day, gradually increasing as mood improves
7. Keep a simple log of mood, anxiety spikes, and sleep to review with clinicians at follow-up visits
8. Consider joining an online or local <med>postpartum support group</med> to reduce isolation and share coping strategies
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Symptoms endorsed
- Persistent low mood, sadness (“gray cloud,” “empty”) daily this week  
- Marked loss of pleasure/enjoyment (laughing feels forced; no anticipation of usual activities)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting competence  
- Generalized anxiety with “what-if” rumination and nocturnal exacerbation  
- Two discrete panic-like episodes (racing heart, breathless, dread)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “can’t keep up,” running on fumes  
- Sleep disturbance driven by anxious/low mood thoughts  
- Frequent crying spells when stressed  
- Passive suicidal ideation (fleeting “what if I weren’t here,” no plan or intent)

Pattern
Symptoms present most days over the past week, interfere with functioning, and appear temporally linked to the postpartum period.

Screening significance
High likelihood of major depressive episode with anxious features; meets threshold for further evaluation for postpartum depression and possible comorbid anxiety disorder.

Risk flags
- Passive suicidal ideation → safety concern; requires immediate risk assessment  
- Significant distress/impairment in caring for infant and self

Next step
Recommend comprehensive psychosocial assessment, safety plan, and discussion of treatment options today.
